extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in film, TV, and cultural criticism (movie-goers and documentary viewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used to evaluate a documentary (specifically one revisiting allegations of sexual misconduct), including scope, evidence, interviewee selection, moral stance, and use of archival material. Useful for critics assessing whether a documentary adds meaningful insight or merely rehashes known facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Moment of release
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the film arrive at a moment when revisiting the story can produce new insight or accountability, versus being so removed that it merely rehashes known facts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes: 'Sorry/Not Sorry comes at a moment that, years after an arc has been established, a real examination of the who, what, where, and why is nothing short of a necessity.' But it also warns that being 'so removed from that ground-zero outing' can mean 'many of the women who were willing to speak out then are no longer compelled to do so now.' If timing is too late, participants decline and the film risks adding nothing new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original insights / new information
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the documentary offer fresh analysis or facts, rather than repeating past reporting and headlines?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review criticizes the film for not pretending 'to have the answers. Or any new insights, to be honest.' A strong film should bring new angles or deeper understanding rather than only jogging memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of examination of power structures
rubrics_metrics.description: How fully does the film investigate the institutional and interpersonal power dynamics that enabled misconduct (management, enablers, industry consequences)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes topics like 'the power structure that enabled such behavior to go unpunished (notably C.K.’s powerful manager Dave Becky) ... feel frustratingly underserved.' Good coverage should explore how power morphed over the subject's career and why victims suffered consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewee selection / who is included or absent
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the key figures, witnesses, and industry peers present and willing to participate, and do notable absences undermine the film's authority?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The film 'asked' every major comic and most declined; 'The abundant omissions of who’s M.I.A. in terms of interviewees start to become glaring' leading to a 'write-around' feeling. A documentary benefits from participation of central figures or clear reasons for their absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and handling of victims' voices and testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the film center and respectfully present the experiences and agency of those harmed, giving them space to tell their stories and demonstrate ongoing impact?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review praises inclusion of Jen Kirkman, Abby Schachner, and Megan Koester, saying 'The inclusion of their voices, their stories, their anger, their refusal to be solely defined by their association with his misconduct ... provides a personal aspect.' Effective documentaries amplify affected voices and show their determination and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of the perpetrator's response and remorse
rubrics_metrics.description: How does the film evaluate or depict the subject's acknowledgment, remorse, or recasting of behavior?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes disappointment that C.K.'s response was 'a defensive recasting of his harassment as a kink and any hint of remorse was AWOL.' A documentary should interrogate the sincerity and content of apologies or defenses rather than presenting them uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of moral stance and where lines are drawn
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the film articulate its own ethical boundaries and make explicit where it believes society should 'draw the line' regarding the artist's misconduct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review states: 'Sorry/Not Sorry needs to do more than just jog our memory. It needs to be a lot clearer about where its own lines are drawn and why this is where ours should be drawn as well.' Strong work stakes a position or explains its criteria for judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of archival material and montages
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the film effectively use clips, routines, appearances, and montages to support its argument rather than substitute for analysis?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece says 'The clips from his routines, TV appearances, and podcast exchanges do a lot of heavy lifting. If you like seeing montages of headlines, you’ll meet more than your daily recommended requirement.' Good documentaries use archival material to illuminate claims, not merely to fill runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filmmaker positionality and editorial balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the filmmakers' own relationships, biases, or generational perspectives acknowledged and balanced, and do they take steps to check their standpoint?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes director Suh's admission she was 'a big fan of C.K.' and that she partnered with a younger filmmaker 'as a way of checking and balancing what seemed “normal” to her then versus now.' Responsible filmmakers should disclose and mitigate personal conflicts that affect framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of corporate and industry aftermath
rubrics_metrics.description: How thoroughly does the film document institutional or corporate responses (e.g., studios severing ties) and their implications?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer finds 'the immediate response after companies like FX severed ties with C.K.' is underserved. A full account should examine consequences and institutional accountability following revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative cohesion and timeline construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the film construct a coherent timeline that connects incidents across the subject's career to illuminate patterns of behavior?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jen Kirkman’s long acquaintance 'allows for a timeline that connects a hell of a lot of dots.' Effective storytelling links events to show continuity or evolution rather than presenting isolated anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asking meaningful questions vs providing answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the documentary pose important questions and also attempt to answer or meaningfully explore them, rather than leaving key issues unresolved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The film 'wants to ask a few questions, such as: Why ... were these accusations suppressed ...? And why was his so-called “cancellation” so brief?' The review notes the filmmakers 'don’t pretend to have the answers,' implying a stronger film should move beyond questions to analysis or conclusions.
